title: Confucian self-cultivation
hookLine: Confucians work on themselves to bring order to home and world (Great Learning)

lines: THE WORLD, THE TOWN, THE KITCHEN.
cards: In a kitchen cupboard sits a set of nesting bowls. The big one holds the middle one, which holds the small one, which holds the smallest, right at the center. Now a different scene.
The news is loud. Something is wrong in the world, something is wrong in your town, and at home a sharp word from this morning still hangs in the kitchen. Where do you even start?
An old Confucian text, the Great Learning, answers with something like those nesting bowls, and it names the one to start with.

teach.h: STATE, FAMILY, SELF: THE CHAIN GOES IN.
teach.b: The Great Learning is short, and its opening is a chain. It speaks of the ancients who wanted bright virtue to shine through the whole realm. To do that, they first ordered their states.
To order their states, they first set their families right. Then the line at the heart of it, in Legge's translation: "Wishing to regulate their families, they first cultivated their persons."
The chain keeps going inward. To cultivate themselves, they made their hearts right. To make their hearts right, they made their thoughts sincere.
To make their thoughts sincere, they extended their knowledge, by looking closely at things.

teach.h: THEN IT RUNS OUTWARD TO PEACE.
teach.b: Then the text runs the chain back outward: things looked into, knowledge complete, thoughts sincere, hearts right, the self cultivated, the family in order, the state well governed, and the whole realm at peace.
The Chinese term at the center is xiushen, cultivating the self.

teach.h: XIUSHEN: TENDING THE SELF LIKE A GARDEN.
teach.b: Cultivate is a farming word in English, and it fits: not a makeover, but slow, daily tending, like a garden. Notice what the text doesn't say. It doesn't say ignore the world.
The goal is still peace for everyone. But the work starts at the smallest bowl.
In paraphrase, it says that from the ruler down to ordinary people, cultivating the self is the root, and when the root is in disorder, what grows from it can't be in order.
For a Confucian, then, tending yourself isn't selfish.
It's the first, and nearest, piece of mending the world.

how: Students of the Confucian tradition read and memorize the Great Learning and treat self-cultivation, through study, reflection, sincere intention and right conduct, as the starting point for good family life and good government.

o: withdrawing from the world to perfect yourself alone
tending your own heart as the root of a peaceful world
a strict exam system for training government officials

s: the Great Learning tells people to ignore the world and fix themselves
the goal is still peace for the whole realm. it says the work starts with the self.
the chain runs inward, then outward again
state, family, self, heart, thoughts, knowledge; then back out to peace in the whole realm.
self-cultivation is only for rulers, in this text
it says, from the ruler down to ordinary people, cultivating the self is the root.

games.q: you want peace in your family. by the Great Learning's chain, where do you begin?
games.why: "wishing to regulate their families, they first cultivated their persons." the chain puts the self beneath the family.

practice: Let your attention come to the smallest bowl: you.
Ask quietly what one small thing in your own life is out of order right now, a cluttered corner, a reply you owe, a grudge you keep feeding, and choose one small enough to put right.
Hold it in mind, picture it done, and let the rest wait its turn.

wordCard.voice: Confucian self-cultivation. Xiushen: tending your own heart, thoughts and conduct, the root from which order in the family and the world can grow. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, from the Great Learning: to cultivate the self.

carryVoice: Your line: start with me. Peace for everyone begins at the smallest bowl. On we go.

sources.q: Wishing to regulate their families, they first cultivated their persons.

sources.ref: The Great Learning, opening text (the full chain, and cultivation of the person as the root)
